scope: Offline source reconciliation. Approval/technical QA/live publication not inferred or queried. Source hashes do not include audio/image bytes; they are not release content versions.

rows.objective: You will ask and answer questions about who, what, and where in a story.
Use clues from the story to figure out what the words don't say. That's an inference!
You will learn to find words that rhyme.
I can ask and answer questions about facts.
I can tell what happened at the beginning, middle, and end of a story.
Characters are WHO a story is about. The setting is WHERE it happens. Events happen in order.
I can be a word detective and figure out new words.
I can tell if a book is make-believe or real.
You will learn who makes the words and pictures in a book!
We will learn how pictures tell us more about a story!
I can tell what happened to both friends, and what happened to just one friend in a story.
I can name what a book is all about and tell important facts.
I can tell why two things go together in a fact.
I can figure out new science words in a fact book.
I can find the front cover, back cover, and title page of a book.
You will learn who makes a fact book: the author writes the true words, and the illustrator makes the pictures or photos!
I can tell what person, place, or thing a fact book picture shows.
I can find the reasons an author gives in a fact book.
I can tell which facts are in both books and which facts are in just one book.
I can find words in a book by reading left to right and top to bottom.
I can find words in a book by reading left to right and top to bottom.
I can find words in a book by reading left to right and top to bottom.
Every big letter has a little letter partner, and you can match them!
I can clap and count the beats in words!
I can slide sounds together to make a word and break a word into its parts!
You will become a super sound detective and find sounds in words.
You will learn to change one sound in a word to make a brand-new word!
You will learn to say the most common sound for consonant letters!
A silent E at the end is quiet, but it makes the vowel say its name.
You will learn to read special words super fast, like a snap!
You will learn to look closely at words and find the letter that changes them.
I can read a story and understand what happens!
I can sort naming words from doing words, and make words mean more than one!
I can make sentences start big and stop strong!
I can learn that some words have two jobs!
You will sort words, find word buddies, and connect words to real life!
You will learn and use position words to tell where things are.
I can ask a question about a story and find the answer in its words.
I can retell a story in order and find its central message.
I can describe a story's characters, setting, and major events using key details.
I can find words in poems and stories that appeal to the senses or show feelings.
I can explain how books that tell stories and books that give information are different.
I can find out who is telling the story at each part.
I can use the words and the picture together to describe a story.
I can compare and contrast what happens to two characters and how each one feels and acts.
I can ask and answer questions about facts in a book.
I can name the main topic of a fact book and retell its key details in order.
I can tell how two facts in a book link together.
I can ask and answer questions about new words in a fact book.
I can use text features to find facts fast.
I can tell if a fact came from the words or the picture.
I can use the words and the picture to describe what a fact page teaches.
I can find the author's point and the reasons that prove it.
I can find facts two books share and facts only one book teaches.
I can spot what makes a sentence just right!
I can blend sounds into whole words, even words with tricky blends!
I can find the first, middle vowel, and last sounds in words, even words with blends!
I can stretch a word and say every sound in order!
I can read a story out loud with a good pace and expression.
I can stop, check, and fix a word that does not make sense.
I can use tools to figure out what a tricky word means.
I can use the other words in a sentence to figure out what a tricky word means.
I can use word parts like un-, re-, and -ful to help me understand new words.
I can find the root word and use endings like s, ed, and ing.
I can pick the word that fits just right.
I can sort words into categories and tell why they belong.
I can tell what a word means by naming its group and one special thing.
I can connect words to real things, places, and moments in my world.
I can pick the verb that matches how it happened.
You will use joining words like because, and, but, and so to connect your ideas.
I can ask and answer who, what, where, when, why, and how questions and prove each answer with the story's words.
I can read a whole fable, retell it in order, and find the moral it teaches.
I can describe how a character responds to major events and challenges in a story.
I can describe how words and phrases give a poem rhythm and meaning.
I can describe how a story's beginning introduces it and its ending concludes the action.
I can notice when two characters feel differently about the same thing and tell who feels what.
I can use the words and the pictures together to understand a story.
I can compare two versions of the same story and tell what stays the same and what changes.
I can read a longer story and understand it using all my reading tools.
I can ask and answer who, what, where, when, why, and how questions about a fact book and prove each answer with the book's exact words.
I can find the main topic of a whole text and the job of each of its paragraphs.
I can explain how the steps in a true text connect, and why their order matters.
I can use the author's help right in the text to figure out what a topic word means.
I can use a fact book's tools to find the facts I need fast.
I can figure out why an author wrote a text.
I can explain how a picture helps me understand the words in an information book.
I can describe how an author's reasons hold up the author's point.
I can compare the most important points of two books about the same topic.
I can read a real fact book and understand it using all my fact-reading tools.
I can pick the right phonics tool and use it to decode long words.
I can hear and see whether a vowel is long or short and read look-alike words correctly.
I can read words with the vowel teams oo, ow, oi, oy, and aw, even when a team makes two different sounds.
I can split a two-syllable word, spot its long vowel patterns, and read it.
I can decode words with prefixes and suffixes: spot the part, read the base, and snap them together.
I can read tricky letter teams by trying one sound, and flipping to the other sound if the word sounds wrong.
I can read heart words by sounding out the fair parts and knowing the tricky part by heart.
I can read smoothly, fix my mistakes, and let the end marks tell my voice what to do.
I can pick a purpose before I read and check that every line makes sense.
I can read out loud with every word right, a just-right speed, and a voice that shows the feeling.
I can catch a word that clunks, reread to fix it, and check that it clicks.
I can solve unknown words with context clues and test both meanings of double-duty words.
I can use sentence clues to figure out a new word, and name the kind of clue.
I can figure out a new word by adding the prefix meaning to a word I know.
I can use a small root word I know as a clue to a big word's meaning.
I can predict what a compound word means by adding the meanings of its two smaller words.
I can use a dictionary or glossary to find what a word means.
I can tell when two words mean almost the same and when they are opposites.
I can connect words to the real things they fit and the places where I would use them.
I can tell how family words climb from weakest to strongest and pick the one that fits.
I can use describing words, thing helpers and action helpers, to make flat sentences come alive.
I can answer a question about a story and point to the exact line that proves it.
I can recount a tale in order, name the message it teaches, and explain how the details show that message.
I can describe a character by her trait, her want, and her feeling, and explain how her action caused what happened next.
I can tell when a phrase in a story means exactly what it says or more than it says, and I can say the plain version.
I can point to a chapter, a stanza, or a scene by its number, and explain how each part builds on the one before it.
I can tell the narrator's view and the characters' views apart from my own view, and back my view with a reason from the story.
I can explain what a picture adds to the words of a story and point to the part of the picture that does it.
I can compare two stories about the same hero by the same author, and tell what stays the same and what changes in the theme, the setting, and the plot.
I can read a whole chapter mostly on my own, hold on to what happens, and use every reading tool I own to understand it from the first page to the last.
I can answer a question about a fact text and point to the exact sentence that says it.
I can find the big idea of a whole fact text, tell which details hold it up, and explain how they back it up.
I can find the words that connect facts in a text and explain how two ideas fit together using because, so, first, or after.
I can work out the meaning of expert words and school words in a fact text, using the supports the text gives me.
I can pick the key words out of a question and use a text's tools to jump straight to the fact I need.
I can tell a fact from the author's opinion in a fact book, find the author's view, and say whether my own view matches it, with a reason.
I can use a map, a photo, and the words of a fact book together to tell where, when, why, and how something happened.
I can name how two sentences or two paragraphs in a fact text connect, by comparison, cause and effect, or sequence, and point to the word that shows it.
I can compare two texts on the same topic by lining up each writer's most important point and key details, and tell what both texts say, what only one says, and how the two points differ.
I can read a whole fact book mostly on my own, hold on to the big idea as it grows, and use every fact-reading tool I own to understand it from the first page to the last.
I can take a long word apart while I read a story and keep the sentence moving.
I can take a big word apart and use its prefix or suffix to unlock what it means.
I can read long words by chunking them, the front cars first and the suffix caboose last.
I can find the vowel spots in a long word, split it into chunks at the right place, and read it chunk by chunk.
I can read words that break the sound rules by sounding out the fair part, learning the heart part by heart, and reading the whole word at a glance.
I can read a real chapter out loud smooth and sure, with the right words, a talking pace, and a voice that follows the marks, so that I understand what happened.
I can name why I am reading before I start, read the page in the way that why needs, and check at the end that the why was met.
I can read a story page and a poem out loud with the right words, a good pace, and expression, and read each one a second time even better.
I can check that every word and every sentence makes sense, and reread to confirm the reading or to correct it.
I can look at a new word, choose the tool that fits it, and test the meaning I get in the sentence.
I can read around a new word, find the clue in the sentence, and prove what the word means.
I can put a known word and a known part together to work out a new word's meaning, then test it in the sentence.
I can find a root I know inside a new word, borrow its meaning, and test it in the sentence.
I can find a word's entry fast, read its parts, and pick the numbered meaning that fits my sentence exactly.
I can decide which connection a question about a word is asking for, then give the saying, the real-life example with a because, the near-same word, or the opposite.
I can tell when a group of words is a saying that means more than it says, find its meaning from the sentence, and use a saying in a sentence of my own.
I can point to a describing word in real life and explain why the example fits.
I can put words about how sure a person is, or how big a feeling is, in order from weakest to strongest, pick the word that fits the clues, and explain the difference between two neighbors.
I can choose and use precise words that tell exactly when and exactly where.
I can answer an explicit question by pointing to the detail, and answer an inference question by citing the detail and saying what it lets me know.
I can name the theme of a story as a big idea about life, prove it with details from across the text, and summarize the story in three sentences.
I can describe a character, a setting, or an event in depth, with a claim and specific details of different kinds from the text.
I can find a word in a story that points to a character from a myth, tell what that character was known for, and explain the meaning the sentence borrows.
I can name prose, a poem, and a drama from the shape of the page, and use the terms for their parts when I talk about a text.
I can find the signal words, name first or third person, say what the narrator can and cannot know, and compare two tellings of one moment.
I can answer an explicit question about a fact text by pointing to the detail or the example, and answer an inference question by citing the detail and saying what it lets me know.
I can state the main idea of a fact text as a full sentence, explain how each key detail supports it, and summarize the text in three sentences.
I can explain an event, a procedure, or a concept in a fact text, telling what happened and why in my own words from specific information in the text.
I can sort a hard word in a fact text into its kind, a field word or an everywhere word, and use that kind's tool to get its meaning.
I can name the overall shape of a fact text or a section of it, point to the signal words that reveal it, choose the diagram that fits, and notice when the text switches shape.
I can tell a firsthand account from a secondhand account of the same event, say what each one focuses on, and find the information only one of them gives.

I can read a four- or five-syllable word inside a sentence by spotting the edges, chunking the middle by ear, saying it and testing it, and flexing a chunk when the first try fails, without stopping the sentence.
I can read an unfamiliar long word by finding the parts I know, choosing the pattern that splits the rest, saying it with one soft chunk, and testing it, inside a sentence or on its own.
I can look at a new word, choose the tool that fits it, test the meaning in the sentence, switch when the test fails, and say which tool I used.
I can find the clue for a new word even when it lives a sentence or a paragraph away, name its kind and its place, and test the meaning.
I can find a Greek or Latin part I know inside a long word, borrow its meaning, add the other part, and test it in the sentence.
I can read words with two-letter teams like the ones in ship, chat, thin, and whale!
I can read a brand new word by saying each sound in order and blending them together!
Silent e and vowel teams make a vowel say its name.
I can count vowel sounds to find the syllables in a printed word!
I can break two-syllable words into chunks and read them!
I can read words with endings like s, ed, and ing!
I can read tricky words that break the sounding out rules.
I can set a purpose before reading, read to answer it, and check that it makes sense.
I can build sentences that sound right when I speak.
I can write names, dates, and sentences the right way.
I can pick the rule breaker words that mean more than one, tell about yesterday, and name a group.
I can use capitals for special names, apostrophes, and letter commas when I write.
I can match my playground voice and my school voice to the listener and the moment.
I can join two ideas with the right word, keep every verb matched to its subject, use the right tense, and compare things correctly.
I can punctuate dialogue, capitalize a title, place the comma in an address, show an owner with an apostrophe, and spell a word when an ending goes on.
I can choose a word or a detail for the effect it makes on a reader, name that effect, and tell which words belong to talking and which belong on the page.
I can understand a story and read some words!
I can read a whole fact book and understand it!
I can read a whole story and a whole poem like a grade one reader.
I can read a whole fact book with purpose and understanding.
I can find words in a book by reading left to right and top to bottom.
